conventions.versions: `jev` lists the Jev versions this catalogue covers, newest last, and `latest` resolves to the newest of them. A check carrying `since` or `until` is run only for the versions in that range; a check carrying neither is run for all of them. One run resolves one version, so a query written for an older Jev is checked against the rules written for it.
conventions.polarity: Every model check is phrased so that a high probability means the defect is present. Nothing in this file inverts that. `question/type-mismatch` is the one check that does not ask about a defect at all: it asks which primitive fits, and `compare: type` turns the weight on a primitive other than the declared one into the probability reported.
conventions.suppress: Answers that do not count as a finding, as data rather than as code, so another implementation reads the same rule. Each entry names the `answer` to suppress and the `when` it holds for. `question_has_fallback_option` is true of a Choice carrying an option that catches whatever the others miss. `question/type-mismatch` needs this: its criteria tell it a catch-all marks a Choice, and it answers `score` on one anyway.
conventions.state: A question-scoped check sees only the question under review, as {instructions, criteria}. Neither the id nor the declared type is shown: Jev never sees the id when the query runs, and naming the type would hand question/type-mismatch its answer.
conventions.trigger: A finding is raised when the probability is above the check's trigger. The probability is reported with the finding; these triggers are defaults, not measurements.
conventions.inconclusive: Set where a reading under the trigger is not evidence the defect is absent, because the readings for clean and defective material overlap. Such a check is reported whether it fires or not, carrying the caveat in `advice`, so a reader sees the limit in the run rather than having to know it. A check without this key means what a cleared reading normally means.
conventions.cost: A model check costs a call and a static rule costs nothing, so a model check that reports what a static rule already reports does not belong in this file. Where the two would find the same thing, the static rule keeps it.
conventions.wordings: A check with `questions` instead of `question` is asked every way at once, in the same call. The wordings mean the same thing, so the mean is the answer and the spread is the error bar. Checks are given a second wording where one wording separated their examples least.
conventions.reads: Which part of the query a check looks at. It decides what the report quotes back and the JSON pointer it reports.
conventions.action: The kind of change the finding asks for: rewrite the text, retype the primitive, restructure into a different shape, which for a compound question means several questions and for criteria means the shape the primitive takes, add something, or remove it.
conventions.suggest: The change to make, written so it holds for any query the check fires on. Where an example follows, it is marked as one: the tool cannot see your query's subject, so a suggestion is guidance, not a patch to paste.
conventions.locate: A check that reads `criteria` may carry a locator, asked in the same call. `locate_mode: each` asks one question per level or option and names every one it fires on, for a fault every element can carry at once. `locate_mode: pick` asks one Choice across them, for a fault one element carries relative to the others.
conventions.removes: Names the node a finding's patch deletes, where deleting one node is the whole fix: `question` for a question that should not be put to Jev at all, `field` for a state field nothing reads.
conventions.severity: How much the defect costs if it is real, not how sure the check is that it is. A choice that should have been a score is reported as advice at a probability of 1.00 because the query still works; a question that asks for arithmetic is an error at 0.97 because the answer will be wrong.
conventions.scope: `question` sees the question under review, `state` the question and the material together, `state-field` one field of it, `state-once` the material alone asked once for the whole query, and `query` the question set, asked once over every pair of questions in it.
conventions.jaggedness: The failure modes TypeSafe documents that a check is written against, as the anchors on its model-jaggedness page. A check can name more than one, because a defect can belong to two modes at once. The README lists each check under one of them, so the table there is a reading of this field and not a copy of it.
conventions.advice: Where `jevlint self-test` shows a check's own suggestion barely clearing its trigger, or unable to clear it at all, the check carries an `advice` note saying so, measured on the examples in checks/fixtures.json. A check with no such note is one whose suggestion cleared its own example with room to spare.

checks.title: Question has no instructions
checks.message: The question has no instructions, so the model is being asked nothing.
checks.hint: Question ids are for your code and are never sent, so an empty instruction reaches the model as nothing at all.
checks.suggest: Put the question in `instructions`: "Does the customer ask for a refund?"

checks.title: Instruction too short to stand on its own
checks.message: The instruction is short enough that it leans on the question id for its meaning.
checks.hint: Question ids are for your code and are never sent, so whatever the id carries does not reach the model.
checks.suggest: Write the question out in full, so `instructions` says what is being asked without `{target}` beside it.

checks.title: Question type is not one Jev answers
checks.message: The question type is not `noul`, `choice` or `score`.
checks.hint: The API answers `noul`, `choice` and `score`, and rejects anything else.
checks.suggest: Set `type` to `noul`, `choice` or `score`.

checks.title: Noul criteria are not a true/false map
checks.message: A Noul's criteria must be a map describing what `true` and `false` mean. A list is rejected with `Input should be a valid dictionary or object to extract fields from`.
checks.hint: A Noul's criteria describe what a yes and a no mean. Any other key is not read.
checks.suggest: Write `criteria` as an object with a `true` and a `false` description, each saying what that answer means. For example, a refund question would read "They ask for money back" as true and "They report a problem without asking for money back" as false.

checks.title: Choice criteria are a list where a map goes
checks.message: A Choice's criteria must be a map of label to description. A bare list is rejected with `Input should be a valid dictionary`.
checks.hint: A bare list is rejected with `Input should be a valid dictionary`. The Choice and Score shapes are exactly inverse, so this is the easiest 422 to hit.
checks.suggest: Write `criteria` as an object keyed by the label you want back, with a description of what belongs under it as the value. For example, a ticket router would key `billing` to "Charges, invoices and refunds" and `technical` to "Something is broken".

checks.title: Choice has fewer than two options
checks.message: A Choice with one option has nothing to choose between.
checks.hint: A Choice settles which option, not whether any applies, so one option settles nothing.
checks.suggest: Add the labels the answer could take, or ask a Noul if the answer is yes or no.

checks.title: Choice has no fallback option
checks.message: None of the options is an `other` or `none of the above`.
checks.hint: Without a catch-all the probability mass has nowhere to go, so it lands on the nearest wrong label. Measured on decision-v7: where the answer was none of the options, removing the catch-all put a mean 0.79 on a label that could not be right and cost a Brier score of 0.660 against 0.349 with it. Where the answer was among the options it cost nothing.
checks.suggest: Add `"other": "Anything the other options do not cover"`.

checks.title: Choice options carry no descriptions
checks.message: Every option is a bare label with no description.
checks.hint: Bare labels are fine where they speak for themselves, and cost you the boundary where the boundary is the thing being judged.
checks.suggest: Give each label a line saying what belongs under it.

checks.title: Score criteria are a map where a list goes
checks.message: A Score's criteria must be an ordered list of levels. A map is rejected with `Input should be a valid list`.
checks.hint: A map is rejected with `Input should be a valid list`. The Choice and Score shapes are exactly inverse.
checks.suggest: Write `criteria` as an ordered array of levels, worst first. For example, an urgency rubric would run "Can wait until next week", "Should be handled today", "The customer is blocked right now".

checks.title: Score has fewer than two levels
checks.message: A rubric needs at least two levels.
checks.hint: A rubric returns a position along its levels, and two is the fewest that describe a direction.
checks.suggest: Add levels until each describes a situation you could recognise in the material.

checks.title: Score has more than ten levels
checks.message: The rubric has more levels than the ten the documentation recommends.
checks.hint: Ten is where the documentation stops, not where the API does. Levels past it are harder to hold apart from their neighbours than they are to send.
checks.suggest: Merge the levels you cannot describe apart from their neighbours.

checks.title: Score levels are bare numbers
checks.message: The levels are bare numbers, so there is nothing in the state for the model to match them against.
checks.hint: The model never sees a level's number or its neighbours, so a bare number gives it nothing to match against. The documented example scores 0.55 at confidence 0.33 with numeric levels and 0.0 at confidence 1.0 with described ones.
checks.suggest: Replace each number with the situation it stands for. For example, a three-level severity rubric becomes "Cosmetic, and nobody's work is affected", "Broken or degraded, but a workaround exists", "No workaround, and the work has stopped".

checks.title: Query asks nothing
checks.message: The query carries no questions.
checks.hint: A request with no questions returns no answers.
checks.suggest: Add at least one question.

checks.title: Two questions ask the same thing
checks.message: Two questions carry identical instructions.
checks.hint: Both ids get the same answer, at the cost of two questions. Two ids do not make two questions.
checks.suggest: Drop one of them, or make the difference explicit in the text of `{target}`.

checks.title: Query carries no state
checks.message: The query has no state, so the state checks were skipped.
checks.hint: The checks that read your state cannot run, so relevance and adversarial content go unmeasured.
checks.suggest: Put a representative `state` in the file. A question is judged against the material it will see, and a query carrying none is checked on its wording alone.

checks.title: State is large
checks.message: The state is large enough that unrelated detail is likely to be costing accuracy.
checks.hint: Retrieve and filter in code first, and send only the fields the questions need. This rule counts characters, which is a proxy for tokens, not a measurement of them.
checks.suggest: Build the state from the fields the questions read, and leave the rest out.

checks.title: The question weighs several factors at once

question.instructions: Answering the question in `instructions` means weighing several separate factors to reach one answer.

criteria.true: The question is broad enough that a reader would balance two or more independent qualities before answering.
criteria.false: The question asks about one quality, which a reader judges on its own.

checks.hint: Ask one question per factor and combine them in code, where you can see and change the weights. One answer carrying several judgements means less, and you cannot tell which factor moved it. Measured on decision-v7's policy cases: joining a second condition that every case already satisfies, so the right answer does not change, still took the answers from 15 of 20 to 11 of 20 and more than doubled the Brier score, and splitting it recovered all of it. That is the largest cost measured for any check here. Accept it where the factors always move together, so no material can satisfy one and not the others, or where the caller wants the blended judgement and will never read the parts: a severity rubric that composites how bad and how urgent is the documented shape, not a defect.
checks.message: Answering this weighs several separate factors to reach one answer.
checks.suggest: Ask one question per factor and weight them in code, so you can see which factor moved the answer. For example, a question about whether to interview someone becomes one about experience, one about the skills the role needs, and one about availability.

checks.title: A yes/no question about a matter of degree

question.instructions: Two careful readers could answer the question in `instructions` differently about the same material, because it turns on a word of degree it never pins down.

criteria.true: The question turns on how much of something there is - heavy, strong, recent, serious - and nothing in the instruction or the criteria says how much is enough.
criteria.false: The question turns on whether something is there at all, or it states the amount that counts.

checks.hint: State the cut-off, or ask a Score instead. A Noul at 0.5 means yes and no are equally likely, not that the answer is halfway. Measured on decision-v7's policy cases and on boolq: the defect is detected and the answers do not move. That is the hardest material available here, and a defect that costs nothing measurable is worth reading rather than failing a build over, so this is advice. Accept it where the boundary is one the reader already shares - a legal threshold, a published service level - so naming it in the question would repeat what the material already settles.
checks.message: This asks yes or no about something that comes in degrees, and never says where the cut-off falls.
checks.suggest: Say where the cut-off falls, or ask a Score over described levels instead. For example, asking whether someone is strong at a language becomes asking whether the CV states they used it at work.

checks.title: The state holds a case the question does not settle

question.instructions: The material in `state` holds a case on the edge of what the question in `question` asks about, and the question does not say which side it falls on.

criteria.true: Something in the state sits on the edge of the question: the thing asked about is mentioned and negated, quoted, hypothetical, partial or part of something larger, or it falls between two of the levels or options on offer. Neither the instructions nor the criteria say where such a case belongs.
criteria.false: Everything in the state falls plainly on one side of the question, or the instructions or the criteria say where the edge case in the state belongs. Material that the question simply does not cover is outside it, not on its edge.

checks.hint: A question is written against the material its author had in mind, and meets the material that arrives. "Does the text contain hello?" reads 0.59 against a state of "not hello", and 0.95 once the criteria say a negated mention still counts, so the defect has a measured cost. The trigger is 0.45 because on twelve paragraphs with an edge planted in them, run twice, the arms that should fire read 0.48 and up and the arms that should not read 0.32 and down. This is advice and not a warning because its rate on clean material is not established: it fires on 5 of the 18 documentation questions that carry a state, the highest rate in this catalogue, and the case for those being real findings instead of false ones is one person reading five queries. Accept it where the edge case is settled by a convention the reader already shares, so naming it in the question would repeat what the material settles.
checks.message: The material holds a case on the edge of what this question asks, and nothing says which side it falls on.
checks.suggest: Name the edge case and say where it belongs, in the instructions or in a criterion. Saying that a negated mention still counts as a mention moved a reading from 0.59 to 0.95 on the same state.
checks.advice: Read this one before acting on it. The rewrite it asks for is measured on one question; how often it points at a query that is already fine is not.

checks.title: The question reaches its subject through another thing
checks.hint: A question about a property of something the reader must first identify costs accuracy on every call. Measured on decision-v7's policy cases and on boolq: the defect is detected and the answers do not move. That is the hardest material available here, and a defect that costs nothing measurable is worth reading rather than failing a build over, so this is advice. Accept it where the hop is inherent because the material decides it: a policy that anchors on purchase in one case and delivery in another has to be read before the date can be.

question.instructions: Answering the question in `instructions` takes more than one lookup: the reader has to find one thing in order to find the next.

criteria.true: The question names its subject as the something-of-a-something, so the reader works inward through a chain of possessives or relative clauses before any judgement can be made.
criteria.false: The question names everything it asks about directly, so the reader finds it in one step. Comparing two things the state already gives is one judgement, not a chain. Naming a field of the state by its path, such as `application.text` or `scheme.threshold`, is a direct name for that field and not a chain either: it says where the material is, and the reader goes straight to it.

checks.message: This reaches its subject through another thing, so one fact has to be settled before the question can be judged.
checks.suggest: Name the thing the question is about directly. Where the hop is unavoidable, ask one question to settle the first fact and a second about the answer, and join them in code.

checks.title: The question stacks negatives
checks.hint: Say it once, positively: ask whether the thing is so, not whether it is not so. Each negative the reader has to cancel out is another place the answer can flip. Measured on decision-v7's policy cases and on boolq, the answers do not move, which is why this is advice rather than a build failure - it is worth reading, not worth blocking on. Accept it where the negative is the domain’s own word and rewording it would change the term of art - "not guilty", "non-compliant" - rather than the sentence around it.

question.instructions: The question in `instructions` puts more than one negative in front of the same thing, so a reader has to cancel them out to see what is being asked.

criteria.true: Two or more negatives stack on one subject - not, never, without, fails to, absent, is it not the case that - and the reader works out what the question means by cancelling them.
criteria.false: The question carries at most one negative, so it reads straight through without cancelling anything out.

checks.message: This stacks negatives, so the reader has to cancel them out before answering.
checks.suggest: Say it once, positively, keeping what `yes` already means: "is it not the case that this falls outside the window" is "is this inside the window". Where saying it positively does flip which answer is which, the code reading the answer has to flip with it, in the same change - a question reworded on its own and a caller left as it was inverts every result and reports nothing.

checks.title: A yes answer means the thing is absent

question.instructions: In the question in `instructions`, a yes answer means the thing being looked for is absent.

criteria.true: The question asks whether material is free of something, lacks something, or otherwise asks the reader to confirm an absence.
criteria.false: A yes answer means the thing being looked for is present.

checks.hint: A high probability then means the thing is missing, and the code that reads it later gets the sense backwards. The harm this names is in the code that reads the answer, not in the answer, so measuring answer quality cannot see it and none is reported here. Accept it where the code reading the answer is written for this polarity and says so; the risk here is a later reader changing one side of that pair without the other.
checks.message: A yes answer here means the thing is absent, which reads backwards in the code that uses it.
checks.suggest: Ask about the thing being present rather than absent: "Is the message free of personal data?" becomes "Does the message contain personal data?". This flips which answer means what, so the code reading it has to flip in the same change - a question reworded on its own and a caller left as it was inverts every result and reports nothing.

checks.title: Answering needs arithmetic

question.instructions: Answering the question in `instructions` needs a number worked out: items tallied, or figures added up.

criteria.true: Answering means producing a number the reader has to work out: tallying items they have to find and count, or adding figures up.
criteria.false: The question asks for a judgment about meaning, and no number has to be worked out to answer it. Comparing one figure with another, or with a threshold, is a reading and not a tally, and asking whether there is more than one of something is a judgment about presence.

checks.hint: Jev recognises the shape of a count instead of tallying, and the error grows with the size of the thing counted. Comparing a figure with a threshold is not this defect: on decision-v7's policy cases Jev answered 30 of 30 threshold questions correctly. Accept it where the count is small, bounded and visible in one place, such as whether a list has more than one entry, and the answer is a judgement about presence rather than the number itself.
checks.message: Answering this needs counting, adding or comparing numbers.
checks.suggest: Do the arithmetic in code. Where the thing being counted is something only a reader can spot, ask one question per candidate and add the answers up yourself.

checks.title: Answering needs dates ordered or subtracted

question.instructions: Answering the question in `instructions` needs two dates or times put in order, or the gap between them measured.

criteria.true: The question asks which came first, how long ago something happened, or whether a date falls inside a window, a quarter or a deadline.
criteria.false: No date or time has to be compared with another to answer the question. Reading a length of time out of the material - how many days a policy allows, how long a warranty runs - is reading a number, not comparing dates, however many dates the sentence mentions. So is extracting one part of a single date, such as its year, month or day.

checks.hint: Jev reads dates as text, not as ordered quantities, and it gets worse with mixed formats and domain boundaries such as quarters or settlement windows. Accept it where the comparison is coarse enough to survive - the same day against months apart - or where you have already moved the arithmetic into code and this question only carries the judgement that is left.
checks.message: Answering this needs two dates put in order, or the gap between them measured.
checks.suggest: Order and subtract the dates in code, using the values you already hold. Where a date is buried in prose, extract each part of it as a Choice over enumerated options first, then do the arithmetic yourself.

checks.title: The question text carries an encoded value

question.instructions: The question in `instructions` is about a value written in an encoded form rather than a named one.

criteria.true: It refers to a hex code, an RGB triple, a byte or binary value, an assembly instruction, a raw identifier, or another encoding a person would decode before judging it.
criteria.false: Everything the question refers to is named in words.

checks.hint: Jev reads `crimson` better than `#DC143C`. This reads the question and not the state, so it finds an encoded value written into the instruction and not one sitting in the material. Both limits are measured: it fires on nothing in the corpus, and asking the same comparison over a reading written plainly and as hex was right 12 of 12 either way, at a Brier of 0.001 against 0.055. The defect is real enough to cost confidence and not, on that test, an answer. Accept it where the encoded value is passed through rather than judged - carried into the answer or matched exactly - so nothing depends on the model decoding it.
checks.message: This asks about a value written in an encoded form.
checks.suggest: Convert the value in code and send the name or the bucket it falls in. For example, a hex colour becomes the colour's name.

checks.title: The question asks for text to be produced
checks.hint: Jev is not trained to generate. Where the answer space is bounded, turn the extraction into a Choice over the candidates and find the candidates with a regex or a generative model. Accept it where the text that comes back is checked before it is used - matched against a regex, a list of known values or a second question - so a wrong answer is caught rather than trusted.
checks.message: This asks for text to be written out instead of for a judgement.
checks.suggest: Turn it into a Choice over the candidates, where the answer is one of a set you can list: asking for a value becomes asking which of these it is. Where the answer is free text with no candidate set, remove the question - that work belongs to a generative model.

questions.instructions: Answering the question in `instructions` means writing text out, in whole or in part.

criteria.true: Some or all of the answer is free text the reader has to put into words: a value read off the material and written out, a reason, a summary, an explanation or a rewrite. Nothing offers it to be chosen.
criteria.false: The whole answer is a judgement about the material, or a choice among candidates `criteria` already lists. A question answerable yes or no is a judgement, however its wording describes what would be written, and choosing a listed candidate is not writing text out.

questions.instructions: Any part of the question in `instructions` asks the reader for words of their own.

criteria.true: One part of the answer is free text the reader supplies, even where another part is a judgement or a choice among candidates `criteria` lists.
criteria.false: Every part of the answer is either a judgement about the material or a choice among the candidates `criteria` lists. A yes-or-no question asks for no words of the reader’s own.

checks.title: Criteria place material the wrong way round

question.instructions: The `criteria` place material the opposite way round from the question in `instructions`.

criteria.true: Material that satisfies the question in `instructions` is placed by `criteria` as not satisfying it, and material that fails the question is placed as satisfying it. The two are about the same property and are the wrong way round.
criteria.false: The `criteria` agree with the question in `instructions`. Criteria about some other property altogether are not this defect however badly they fit: reversing them would not make them agree, so there is nothing here to swap.

checks.hint: Swap the two descriptions so `true` says what makes the answer yes. The criteria are read as an extension of the instruction, and TypeSafe's jaggedness page says a Noul whose `true` maps to no performs worse, without giving a figure. Measured on decision-v7's imdb rows, inverting them cost nothing: 19 of 20 right either way. Twenty rows of one easy binary task is thin, and it is the only measurement there is, so this is a warning rather than an error. Accept it where the inversion is deliberate and the code reading the answer inverts with it, and say so in the reason so the next reader does not undo one half of the pair.
checks.message: The criteria place material the opposite way from the instruction.
checks.suggest: Swap the descriptions so each says what that answer means for the question as asked. A `true` description says what makes the answer yes.

checks.title: Criteria decide on something else

question.instructions: The `criteria` decide on a different property from the one `instructions` asks about.

criteria.true: The descriptions turn on something the question never raised, so material could answer the question one way and be placed by a property it does not mention.
criteria.false: Every description is about the property the question asks about, whether or not it draws the line where you would. Criteria that set out the rule for a judgement the question leaves open are not this defect: a question asking whether an application needs review, with criteria naming the income above which it does, is the author saying where the line falls.

checks.hint: The criteria are read as the second half of the instruction, so a description about another property replaces the question rather than sharpening it. Accept it where the criteria set out the rule for a judgement the question leaves open, such as naming the income above which an application needs review.
checks.message: The criteria decide on a property the instruction did not ask about.
checks.suggest: Write each description in terms of the thing the instruction asks about. Where the other property matters too, it is a second question.

checks.title: Another primitive fits these answers better

question.instructions: Look at the answers this question asks for: the ones `criteria` names, or, where there are no `criteria`, the ones the question in `instructions` implies. How do they relate to each other?

criteria.noul: There are two of them, and they stand for yes and no, or for a thing being present and being absent.
criteria.choice: They name separate kinds of thing, with no sense in which one is higher or lower than another. An option that catches whatever the others miss, such as `other` or `not_stated`, means these are kinds and not steps: a catch-all has no place on a scale.
criteria.score: They are steps along one quality, running from less of it to more of it.
criteria.other: The answer is not among them at all: it is a value the reader would have to write down, such as a name, a number or a date.

checks.hint: Where two types both fit, prefer the one your code can act on directly. A Noul at 0.5 means yes and no are equally likely, not that the answer is in the middle. Accept it where the primitive is chosen for the caller rather than the question: a Noul whose probability you threshold, where a Choice would give you a label you would only threshold anyway.
checks.suggest: Change `type` to the primitive named, and reshape `criteria` to match it: a map of label to description for a Choice, an ordered list of described levels for a Score, a `true` and `false` pair for a Noul. Where no primitive is named, the answer is a value to be read out of the material rather than a judgement about it, so take the question out and read the value in code.

checks.title: Levels name degrees of a quality

question.instructions: The levels in `criteria` name degrees of a quality rather than describing situations.

criteria.true: Levels read as low, moderate, high, severe, very severe, or as bare numbers, so there is nothing concrete in the material to match them against.
criteria.false: Each level describes a situation specific enough to recognise, such as "broken or degraded, but a workaround exists".

checks.hint: Write each level as the situation that puts material there, not as a grade. A level reading `moderate` has nothing behind it: the model never sees a level's neighbours, so it has nothing to place the material against. Measured on decision-v7's sentiment rows, where the levels run from `very negative` to `very positive`, this fires on all twenty and the rewrite does not help - two made blind put 10 of 20 reviews on the labelled level against 12 of 20 for the degrees. A rubric whose subject is itself a degree is the case to accept this finding on.
checks.message: The levels name degrees of a quality instead of describing situations.
checks.suggest: Replace each level with the situation it stands for, concrete enough to recognise in the material. For example, a level reading "moderate" becomes one naming what is broken and what still works.
checks.locate: This level names a degree of a quality instead of describing a situation: {element}

checks.title: A level requires two qualities that can hold apart

question.instructions: At least one level in `criteria` requires two qualities that can hold independently of each other.

criteria.true: A level requires two qualities that could each be high or low without the other changing, such as experience and punctuality, or lateness and damage, so material with one and not the other fits no level on the scale.
criteria.false: The levels run along one axis, however many clauses each is written in. Clauses that together fix one position on that axis - "the same day but after the window" locates one degree of lateness - are one quality, and so is a condition named with its consequence, its cause or its mitigation.

checks.hint: One dimension per Score. Split it and weight the scores in code; the weights are yours to change without touching a prompt. Measured on decision-v7's sentiment rows: joining a second quality that varies across the levels cost 4 placements in 20 and nearly doubled the squared error, while joining one that asks the same of every level cost nothing. This fires equally hard on both, so a second quality that is constant across the scale is a finding worth accepting with that reason.
checks.message: A level names two qualities joined together, so material with one and not the other fits no level.
checks.suggest: Split it into one Score per quality and weight them in code.
checks.locate: Which of these levels names two qualities joined together?
checks.advice: Blind testing found two-axis rubrics reading 0.72 to 0.80 and published-correct rubrics reading 0.62 to 0.76, so the two overlap and no trigger separates them. At 0.77 this fires on none of the published-correct material and on fewer than half the two-axis rubrics: a clear reading is not evidence the scale measures one quality.

checks.title: Two levels a reader could not choose between
checks.hint: Levels are evaluated separately, so a level said twice splits the probability and drags the expectation to a point neither copy describes. A partial overlap, where two levels share ground without restating each other, reads well below the trigger and is not what this finds. Accept it where the levels are separated by a threshold the material states, so a reader with the material in front of them can always tell which applies.
checks.message: Two of the levels describe the same situation in different words.
checks.suggest: Merge them, or move the boundary so each level claims ground the others do not.
checks.locate: Which of these levels restates another one in the list?

question.instructions: Two of the levels in `criteria` are ones a reader could not choose between.

criteria.true: Two levels say the same thing in different words, or everything one of them asks for is also asked for by another, so material fitting one fits the other and nothing in it decides which.
criteria.false: Each level asks for something no other level asks for, so material meeting one fails the rest, even where the boundary between two neighbouring levels is a matter of degree.

checks.title: Two options describe the same material
checks.hint: Overlapping options split the probability between them, so the winning label can lose to an option neither reading supports. Accept it where the overlap is deliberate and the caller reads the spread rather than the winner, or where the options are a published taxonomy you cannot change.

questions.instructions: A reader could file the same material under two of the named options in `criteria` and be right both times.

criteria.true: Two named options overlap: they describe the same thing in different words, or one is a narrower case of the other, so the same input satisfies both descriptions.
criteria.false: No two named options can both be right about one input. An `other` or `none of the above` option is not an overlap, because it is only what the named options leave behind. Options that name points along one quality, such as calm, frustrated and angry, are a scale and not an overlap; a Choice doing a Score's job is a different defect.

questions.instructions: Some material would honestly fit two of the named options in `criteria` at once.

criteria.true: Two named options share ground, either because they cover the same territory or because one sits wholly inside the other, so a reader picking between them is guessing at which was meant.
criteria.false: Every named option claims ground no other named option touches. An `other` or `none of the above` option is not an overlap, because it is only what the named options leave behind. Options that name points along one quality, such as calm, frustrated and angry, are a scale and not an overlap; a Choice doing a Score's job is a different defect.

checks.message: Two of the named options cover the same ground.
checks.suggest: Merge them, or narrow each description so the same input cannot sit under both.
checks.locate: Which of these options covers ground that another named option already covers, or sits wholly inside it?

checks.title: A state field no question needs: `{field}`

question.instructions: The field named `{field}` is beside the point of the question in `question`.

criteria.true: The question turns on material held elsewhere, and this field is about something else.
criteria.false: Answering the question needs something this field holds.

checks.hint: Unrelated detail acts as a distractor, and a larger state makes a wrong answer harder to trace. Size is not what costs an answer: on decision-v7's policy cases the answers hold at one line of spare field, at 14,000 characters of it, and where the field holds another claim reading like the one being asked about, and a language router holds at 4,851 characters of unrelated English. The same router loses eight of its thirteen accepted-correct answers to 414 characters of Japanese, because it asks which language a text is written in and the spare field is text. Nothing here reads that pairing, so this is advice at every size, and a field worth acting on is one whose content is what the question judges. Accept it where the field is carried for something other than this query - an audit trail, a downstream consumer, a field you are about to start reading.
checks.message: The field `{field}` holds nothing the questions read.
checks.suggest: Leave `{field}` out of the state, or build the state from the fields each question needs.

checks.title: The state carries an instruction to whoever reads it

question.instructions: Some passage in `state` instructs whoever is assessing the material, rather than arguing to them.

criteria.true: A passage tells whoever assesses the material what to record, what to disregard, or how to answer - directing the assessment instead of putting a case to it. Wording such as "record this as", "treat this as" or "do not count" addressed to the assessor is this defect wherever it sits.
criteria.false: A passage puts a case to its reader, however forcefully. A covering letter, an appeal, a submission, a reference or a review is written by its author to persuade, and making a case, praising the subject or asking for a particular outcome is the document doing its job. A question with its instructions and criteria is written to direct a judgement and is not planted; where the state holds one, that is the material itself.

checks.hint: Jev does not treat state as hostile, so an instruction planted in user-written content can move the answer. Nothing you write in the query removes the text, so this reports a property of the material you are sending, not a defect you can edit away. Accept it where the material is expected to argue and you know it: a file of appeals or references is doing its job, and the reading tells you what kind of document arrived.
checks.message: Something in the state addresses whoever is judging it, and could steer the answer.
checks.suggest: Say in the criteria exactly what the decision turns on, so an instruction planted in the material has nothing to attach to. The finding stays, because the text stays, and tight criteria narrow what it can do without removing it. Once the criteria are tight, accept the finding in `.jevlint.json` with that as the reason.
checks.locate: Which of these parts of the state carries the text aimed at whoever is judging it?
checks.advice: This suggestion cannot clear the check. It hardens the question, and the check reads the state, which is unchanged. Act on it and accept the finding with that reason.

checks.title: The question is built on a record the state does not hold
checks.hint: A question built on a record the state never carries still comes back with a probability. Check this against the states you send, not a tidy example. Accept it where the state legitimately varies and the caller already gates on another question that says whether the record is there.

questions.instructions: The question in `question` is built on a record that sits outside the material in `state`.

criteria.true: The state holds unrelated records, and the one the question is built on sits outside them, so an answer would be invented rather than read.
criteria.false: The state holds the record the question is built on. A question, with its own instructions and criteria, is such a record where that is what the state carries. Where the question asks whether something appears inside the record, a state showing it does not appear has answered the question.

questions.instructions: A reader given only the material in `state` would have to invent something before the question in `question` could be answered.

criteria.true: The record the question is built on is missing from the state, so the reader would supply it from imagination.
criteria.false: The state carries what the reader needs. Finding that the thing the question looks for is absent from it is an answer, not an invention.

checks.message: The question is built on a record this state does not carry.
checks.suggest: Send the record your question turns on - the thing it asks about - so the state carries what the question needs. Where a state legitimately does not have it, skip the question for that state instead of asking it anyway: an answer to a question the material cannot settle is a number with nothing behind it.

checks.title: Noul does not say what yes and no mean
checks.message: The question carries no criteria, so where the line between yes and no falls is left to the model.
checks.hint: The instruction is enough for many Nouls. Where the boundary is subtle, saying what a yes and a no mean is what moves a question from guessing to deciding.
checks.suggest: Add a `criteria` object with a `true` and a `false` description, saying which material counts as each.

checks.title: Two questions ask for the same judgement
checks.message: Two questions in this query ask for the same judgement in different words.
checks.hint: Both answers cost a question and move together, so the second buys nothing, and where they disagree the disagreement is noise rather than information. Accept it where the two questions are asked of different parts of the state, so the same words are a different question each time.
checks.suggest: Keep the one whose answer your code acts on and drop the other. Where the two are meant to differ, make the difference explicit in both.

question.instructions: These two questions ask for the same judgement about the same material: {pair}

criteria.true: A reader who answered one would have answered the other, because both turn on the same thing.
criteria.false: The two turn on different things, even where both are asked about the same material.

checks.title: Criteria are a plain value
checks.message: `criteria` holds a plain value. Jev wants a map for a Noul or a Choice and a list for a Score, and rejects anything else.
checks.hint: A comma-separated string looks like options to a reader and is one string to the API.
checks.suggest: Write the options out as JSON: a map of label to description for a Choice, an ordered list of levels for a Score.

checks.title: Choice has no options
checks.message: A Choice with no `criteria` gives the model nothing to choose between.
checks.hint: The labels are what comes back, so a Choice without them has no answer to return.
checks.suggest: Add a `criteria` object keyed by the label you want back, with a description of what belongs under it.

checks.title: Score has no levels
checks.message: A Score with no `criteria` has no rubric, so there is nothing for a reading to be a position on.
checks.hint: A Score answers with a position on the levels you give it. Without them there is no scale.
checks.suggest: Add a `criteria` array of described levels, ordered worst to best.

checks.title: A level is not a description
checks.message: A level holds an object or a list where the rubric needs a sentence the model can match against.
checks.hint: A level is matched against the material as text. A nested structure has no reading.
checks.suggest: Write each level as one sentence naming the situation it stands for.

checks.title: The type is not written the way the API takes it
checks.message: `type` is matched exactly, so a capitalised primitive is rejected.
checks.hint: The linter reads the type case-insensitively so it can still check the question. The API does not.
checks.suggest: Write `type` in lower case.

checks.title: The instructions carry no words
checks.message: `instructions` holds a structure with nothing readable in it, so the model is sent no question.
checks.hint: Instructions can be an object putting the question beside the data it refers to, but something in it has to be the question.
checks.suggest: Put the question itself in `instructions`, as a string or as a field of the object.

checks.title: The request carries a key the API does not take
checks.message: A key at the top of the request that is not `state`, `questions` or `model` is rejected.
checks.hint: The API refuses an unknown top-level key outright, with `api_usage_error` and no indication which one.
checks.suggest: Take it out of the request. Settings that belong to your own tooling go beside the query, not inside it.

checks.title: The request names a moving build
checks.message: The request names a build by an alias, which resolves to whichever build is newest when it runs.
checks.hint: A report describes the build it was taken against, and a request naming an alias runs against whichever build is newest, so the two come apart the day a new one lands. `jev-latest` answers as `jev-1.13.0`, the build this catalogue is written for, so nothing is wrong with such a request today. Accept it where you want new builds without a deploy and have something else watching for the answers moving.
checks.suggest: Name the build, as `jev-1.13`, and raise it when you have measured the new one.

checks.title: An option's description is not text
checks.message: An option's description holds a number, a list or a null where the API takes a string.
checks.hint: A description is matched against the material as text, and anything else is rejected before the model sees it.
checks.suggest: Write each description as a sentence saying what belongs under that label.

checks.title: Question depends on another question's answer
checks.message: This question is written to use something another question in the same request produces.
checks.hint: Questions in one request are independent, so what this names is not there to be read and the question is answered as though the material were absent. Measured on decision-v7's contrastive rows: with the policy the question needs moved out of the state and into another question's instructions, the label is answered 20 of 30 against 27 of 30 with it in the state, at a Brier score of 0.237 against 0.064. Deleting the policy outright reads 20 of 30 and 0.242, so a sibling carries nothing. Accept it where the phrase points at the material rather than at an answer the request has to produce.
checks.suggest: Put what the question needs into the state. Where the second question cannot be built until the first is answered, send it as a second request.

question.instructions: The question names another question in the request, or an answer to one.

criteria.true: Answering it needs a result the request has to produce first, such as an earlier answer, a classification already made, or a question named by its id.
criteria.false: It asks only about the material it is given. A phrase pointing at that material, such as the policy above or the case as described, is the material and not another question.

checks.title: Choice has more than 255 options
checks.message: A Choice takes at most 255 options and this one has more.
checks.hint: The request is refused before the model sees it, with a 400 and `Too many choices. Must have at most 255 choices.` A list this long is usually a table the code already holds, and the question is which row the material points at.
checks.suggest: Narrow the list to the labels this material can take, or ask in two steps: a Choice over the groups, then one over the members of the group it picked.

checks.title: The answer follows from the material by a rule
checks.message: Code holding the material could answer this without a model.
checks.hint: Measured over 96 answers on generated states, Jev got every one right, so what this costs is not accuracy: it is a call, a round trip and a probability where code gives a fact, paid on every request for as long as the question is in the query. Asked both ways over nineteen questions, a field lookup reads 0.73 and up and a question needing a reading of the material reads 0.42 and down. A date comparison reads 0.64 and an encoded value 0.69, so a question carrying one of those defects can draw this as well as the check written for it. Accept it where the field the rule would read is not reliably there or not reliably shaped, and where the value is stated in prose rather than carried in a field, because then code has to read the material before it can apply any rule.
checks.suggest: Take the question out and apply the rule in code to the field it reads.

questions.instructions: Code holding the material could answer this question by itself, with no model.

criteria.true: The question names a value and a test to apply to it, so the answer is looked up or compared rather than judged.
criteria.false: The question asks what the material means, describes or amounts to. Naming a field does not make it mechanical: asking what a field says about something is still a judgement. Arithmetic to work out, a date or time comparison, and a value written in an encoding a reader would decode are each a different defect with a check of their own.

questions.instructions: Answering this means applying a rule to a value, not reading the material.

criteria.true: The question names a field or a value in the material and a test to apply to it - an equality, a threshold, a membership, a substring, whether it is filled in - so the answer is that test applied to that value.
criteria.false: Answering means reading the material rather than testing a value in it: what it means, what it describes, or a fact somebody has to find in prose before they can state it. One right answer does not make a question mechanical, and neither does naming a field: code can apply a rule to a value handed to it, not read a document to find the value first. Arithmetic to work out, a date or time comparison, and a value written in an encoding a reader would decode are each a different defect with a check of their own.

checks.title: Option keys a JavaScript caller reorders
checks.message: An option key is written the way an array index is, so a JavaScript caller sends the options in an order this file does not carry.
checks.hint: A JavaScript object lists a key that looks like an array index before every other key, and lists those in ascending numeric order however they were written. jevlint reads your file with a parser that keeps the order you wrote, so the order it checks is not the order such a caller sends. How far option order moves a Choice answer is not settled: reversing the options changed no pick over the 24 cases measured for this catalogue. Accept it where nothing between this file and the API builds the options as a JavaScript object.
checks.suggest: Give each key a form no language reads as a number, as `hour_06` for `06`, and leave the descriptions as they are.

checks.title: A Choice over an outcome the material does not settle
checks.message: The options name an outcome the material does not settle, so the probability beside the answer is not a likelihood.
checks.hint: A Choice reports a probability for the option it picks, and over an outcome the material cannot settle that number is not a likelihood. Measured outside this repository, by jev-does-not-play-dice: on a hidden fair die roll a mean 0.83 on the picked face against a chance of 0.17, with accuracy at 19.0% over 400 calls, and on a coin 0.92 at 52.0% accuracy. The same die asked as a Noul read 0.19, so what the number is worth follows from the primitive and not from the question. The trigger is 0.70 because over the four draws that project recorded and two outcomes written here this reads 0.83 and up, while over fourteen Choice questions whose material does settle them it reads 0.53 and down. The reading nearest the line is a question about what somebody wants, which the material leaves unstated, so a finding on one of those is the one to read rather than act on. Accept it where you read the label and never the number beside it.
checks.suggest: Where you act on the probability, take the question out: no primitive reports a likelihood for an outcome the material does not settle. Where you act on the label alone, keep the question and leave the number unread.

question.instructions: Picking between the options in `question` is guessing, as far as the material in `state` goes.

criteria.true: The options name results of something the material presents as still open, or as already settled and withheld from whoever reads it, so one option is as good a pick as another.
criteria.false: The material bears on the answer, so picking between the options is reading it. A question about what somebody wants, intends, means or is likely to do is such a case, however little the material says about it, and so is one whose answer the material states as a number or a forecast.
